facts.claim: Only 36% of the replicated studies achieved statistical significance, while 97% of the original studies reported statistically significant results.
facts.quote: Although statistically significant results were reported in 97% of the original studies, statistical significance was achieved in only 36% of the replicated studies.

facts.claim: More than 90% of tests performed in eligible psychology experiments tested negligible effects.
facts.quote: The resulting model suggests that more than 90% of tests performed in eligible psychology experiments tested negligible effects

facts.claim: Replication effects were half the magnitude of the original effects.
facts.quote: Replication effects were half the magnitude of original effects, representing a substantial decline.

facts.claim: Both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions about reproducibility are possible, and neither are yet warranted.
facts.quote: Using the Reproducibility Project: Psychology data, both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions about reproducibility are possible, and neither are yet warranted.

facts.claim: Correlational tests suggest that replication success was better predicted by the strength of original evidence than by characteristics of the original and replication teams.
facts.quote: Correlational tests suggest that replication success was better predicted by the strength of original evidence than by characteristics of the original and replication teams.

research.angle: Large-scale replication projects found that only 36% of psychology experiments achieved statistical significance, though some researchers argue that neither optimistic nor pessimistic conclusions are yet warranted.
research.verdict: The evidence shows a substantial decline in replication success compared to original findings, with many tests appearing to yield negligible effects.
research.caveat: One source notes that both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions about reproducibility are possible and neither are yet warranted.
